The influence of the design parameters — sulfur mass, internal heat exchanger pipe diameter and pitch ratio or specific surface area — on the dynamic charge and discharge performance of the system, and system cost (using cost model discussed in Task 5.0) was analyzed to identify feasible design window that meets the following performance and cost targets of G/NG- 2D - Performance targets: Peak charge rate – 2×discharge rate (corresponding to solar multiple of 3.0), charge time ≤ 8 h, Effective discharge time (𝑡∗) = (Energy discharged 𝐷 during cyclic operation /𝑄̇ ) ≥ 10 h; Storage cost target: C < 45 (±2.5) $/kWh where 𝐼𝑃𝐻 TES C is based on the energy discharged during the daily cyclic operation. TES Initially, the system is in a fully discharged state at temperature of 140 oC and charging takes place as hot HTF corresponding to charge rate of 2×𝑄̇ flows through the internal 𝐼𝑃𝐻 heat exchanger to transfer heat to sulfur. The maximum HTF flow rate through the system based on allowable pressure drop and pumping constraints were imposed. The charging process was simulated for a maximum target duration of 8 hours. Following the charge process, the discharge process was simulated for a total duration of 16 hours to complete daily cycling. During the discharge process, as HTF exit temperature decreases, the HTF flow ramps up — controlled by adjusting the speed of the pump using a variable frequency drive — to meet the desired constant heat rate. Once the HTF exit temperature reached a certain minimum discharge cut-off temperature (𝑇′), part heat load was provided by the 𝐷 sulfur TES with the rest supplied by the back-up boiler (Figure 2). The discharge cut-off temperature is dictated by the maximum HTF flow rate allowable due to pressure drop considerations and the design surface area of the oil to steam heat exchanger. In this analysis, 𝑇′ was taken to be 20 oC above the required steam saturation temperature 𝐷 based on the trade-off between cost and performance. During the cyclic operation, the charging temperature profile of the first process becomes the initial condition of the subsequent discharge process which in turn becomes the initial condition of the next charge process and so on. Cyclic charge and discharge simulations were conducted until a periodic quasi-steady state is reached, when the variations in performance metrics and model output from one cycle to another are less than 0.5%. The corresponding combinations of the optimum design parameters and the performance metrics are tabulated in Table 6 for the different scenarios investigated. The optimal design configuration listed in Table 6 results in sulfur TES Cost of ~ 36 $/kWh for 12 bar 188 oC IPH and ~ 27 $/kWh for 3 bar 140 oC IPH for effective discharge duration ≥ 10 h.
